text: Senator-elect Troy Jackson backs Van Hollen over Schumer for Senate majority leader

Senator-elect Troy Jackson, of Maine, has endorsed Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader, a blow to the current minority leader, Chuck Schumer, ahead of a vote among Senate Democrats next Tuesday.

The Maryland senator has successfully cast himself as a “change” candidate following Democrats’ sweeping success in the midterms, whereas Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for the last decade, is seen as the “establishment” figure in the race, representing the status quo.

Van Hollen and the argument for a new generation of leadership has received backing from Bernie Sanders, incoming senators Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan and others, as well as some celebrity backing from the likes of Robert De Niro, Jane Fonda, and others.

“I’ve talked with Mainers about what they need from the Senate, and I believe it’s time for a change in leadership. I’ll be voting for Senator Van Hollen,” Jackson said in a statement. “When we spoke, I told him Maine needs a seat at the table when the caucus decides what gets funded and what we’re going to fight for. I was impressed by his vision for the caucus, and I came away confident he’ll take Maine’s priorities seriously.

“From one end of Maine to the other, I heard the same thing. People are working harder, falling further behind, and getting tired of being told to wait. Senator Van Hollen and I agree that it’s time to end the filibuster, pass Medicare for All, and give working people a raise by increasing the minimum wage. I want a leader who’ll bring those fights to the floor and make every senator say where they stand.
“Mainers voted for change in November, and they ought to get it. Whoever leads this caucus, I’ll fight like hell to make sure the Senate takes on the problems Mainers sent me to Washington to solve.”
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:

Trump administration tries to blame Obama for explosives in Iowa US army was concerned about in 2004

Faced with criticism for the US army’s potentially hazardous detonation on Wednesday of a stockpile of the bomb-making material lead azide in Middleton, Iowa, the Trump administration made a concerted effort on Wednesday to place the blame on former president Barack Obama.
In public comments, Donald Trump, JD Vance and Stephen Miller, all claimed, without evidence, that the hazardous explosives were improperly stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in 2009.

They made this claim despite the fact that the US army said in a 2014 publication still available online that a project to move away from the use of lead azide “started in 2004 in response to the Department of Defense’s concerns over a 40-year-old stockpile of lead azide deteriorating at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.”
In 2004, Obama was an Illinois state lawmaker running for the US Senate and George W Bush was president.

The White House did not reply to a request to explain how it came to the conclusion that a problem identified in 2004 could be called “a dangerous mess the Obama Administration left behind,” or say what action the first Trump administration took to address the problem between 2017 and 2021.

The dangers of the lead azide at the Iowa plant were noted decades earlier, in a report from the US army’s toxic and hazardous materials agency, published in January 1980, when Jimmy Carter was president and Obama was a freshman in college. The report explained that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,700 canisters containing lead azide were destroyed there.
Nonetheless, Rob Cekada, the director of the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives claimed on Wednesday, “we were handed a problem frankly that started in 2009”.

“We learned that these lead azide explosives were brought here from a stockpile outside of the Middleton area and transported here to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and placed in the earthen-covered magazines, H2 and H3,” Cekada added, without offering any explanation of what his assertion was abased on.

“At the time those records showed that these were already old, degraded lead azide explosives and were already a concern for the military at that time,” he went on, again failing to explain what records he was referring to. “Unfortunately, under that administration, nothing was done to handle that issue.”

“This administration came together quickly in March of 2026, developed a plan to properly mitigate the threat caused by these explosives,” Cekada, a former police officer with no military background said.

A day earlier, Cekada told reporters: “from what we’ve learned, in about 2009 the nation’s stockpile was moved here to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. That stockpile contained approximately 10,000 pounds. Some of that lead azide was already 60-plus years old, and in many cases it was noted that there was some deterioration, in 2009.”

Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law group that challenged the detonation permit given to the army by the Environmental Protection Agency, told the Guardian that the same claim was made in a sworn declaration filed in court on Monday by a senior military officer. In that declaration, Major General Eric P. Shirley told the court: “The lead azide has been stored at IAAAP since 2009”.
Senator Chris Van Hollen calls out Trump administration 'lies' about Kilmar Ábrego Garcia

Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who played a central role in helping his undocumented constituent Kilmar Ábrego Garcia fight his unlawful deportation to El Salvador last year, denounced the Department of Homeland Security for making unsubstantiated allegations about Ábrego on social media on Wednesday.

Ábrego voluntarily left the United States on a flight for Spain on Tuesday night, bringing an end to the 20-month legal battle that followed his wrongful deportation to El Salvador, in violation of a court order.
In an interview with CSPAN earlier on Wednesday, Van Hollen said that he spoke with Ábrego and his wife, Jennifer, who is a US citizen, shortly before the boarded a flight from Madrid.

“What the Trump administration has been trying to do for the last year and a half is engage in a vendetta against Kilmar Ábrego Garcia because he stood up for his constitutional rights,” Van Hollen added. “So they brought a malicious and vindictive prosecution against him and they tried to force him to go to a country or countries that have records of human rights abuses. They essentially tried force him into one of those countries and punish him because he’d stood up for his constitutional rights. They were forced to back down from that.”
On Wednesday, the senator, who is running to lead the new Democratic majority in the Senate, responded to a post from the DHS calling Ábrego a gang member, writing:

double quotation markLies, lies & more lies from the same folks who called Renee Good & Alex Pretti “terrorists” after they were gunned down by DHS agents. Your “goal” was for Kilmar to rot forever in a gulag & deny him the due process he, & every person in this country, is owed under our Constitution. As I said from day 1, this was never about Kilmar, it was about his rights. It is BECAUSE we fought to protect his rights that all of ours are a little safer today.

The incoming US House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, said on Wednesday that the new Democratic majority in Congress must “move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran; not simply in the first 100 days, but during the first 100 hours.”
Jeffries made the comment in an interview with Ben Meiselas, a founder of MeidasTouch, an influential progressive podcast network.

Meiselas also asked Jeffries to commit, on-camera, to a list of 14 legislative priorities so that they could do another interview at the end of next year “and see what was it that the House Democrats accomplished”.
Here is the list of policies Jeffries committed to pursue in 2027:
pass the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act, which the AFL-CIO says “restores the right of workers to freely and fairly form a union”;
advance a constitutional amendment to overturn the Citizens United ruling that undermined campaign finance spending limits;
advance legislation toward universal health care;
ban partisan and mid-decade gerrymandering;
ban congressional stock trading;
raise the federal minimum wage;
repeal Trump’s tariffs';
reverse Medicaid and SNAP cuts;
restore Affordable Care Act tax credits;
reform the immigration system and pass the Dream and Promise Act;
pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and combat voter suppression;
claw back billions in ICE funding;
enact major Supreme Court reform.
Trump's efforts to rollback birthright citizenship face latest setback
A federal judge has barred the Trump administration from restricting the birthright citizenship of babies born in the US to foreign government workers.

“Children born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are American citizens from birth. That rule, enshrined in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and codified in the Immigration and Nationality Act, derives from the English common law and is deeply rooted in our legal tradition,” US district judge Christopher Cooper wrote in a Wednesday opinion.
The ruling comes months after the Supreme Court blocked an executive order, where Trump sought to deny automatic citizenship for US newborns, whose parents were not citizens.
The president signed new executive orders in August with a narrowed scope, targeting the infants of foreign diplomats and members of “foreign terrorist organizations.”
That directive was also aimed at people engaged in birth tourism, a practice where people travel solely to the US for the purpose of giving birth and securing citizenship for their child.
Although birth tourism represents a small portion of annual births, it has been touted often in Trump’s case against automatic citizenship.
Former vice-president Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town.

The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said yesterday that it will sell the paper to Gore in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith County in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles east of Nashville.

As the beleaguered news industry struggles with newspaper closures and growing news deserts, Gore characterized the purchase as a move that preserves an independent local voice in Carthage and Smith County.

“Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the [Nashville] Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Gore said in a statement to the Associated Press.

Before entering politics, Gore spent six months as a military reporter in the US army during the Vietnam War. He returned to Tennessee and worked for a few years as an investigative reporter at The Tennessean before running for Congress in 1976.

Gore, a Democrat, represented Tennessee in both chambers of Congress, served as Bill Clinton’s vice-president from 1993 to 2001, and ran for president twice. After losing the 2000 presidential election to George W Bush, he went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate activism. He also narrated and was the subject of the Academy Award-winning documentary film “An Inconvenient Truth”.

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said today. The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. My family and I decide our future.” Read Ashifa Kassam’s report here.

JD Vance said that Jensen Huang, the recently reinstalled Nvidia CEO, was never under criminal investigation and therefore did not need a pardon after Donald Trump said he would be open to offering one to the tech executive. The vice-president told reporters he supported Huang being reinstated after receiving “assurances” from the attorney general, Todd Blanche, and other top US officials that Huang was “under no investigation”. Trump and Vance intervened in Nvidia’s leadership drama and put pressure on the tech company’s board to reinstall Huang despite other lawmakers’ concerns over whether he posed a national security risk for having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Ariana Baio has the story.

Indeed, the US justice department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations Huang conducted an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Reuters reported. Instead, Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the DOJ’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said Reuters’ sources.

Trump administration approves Elon Musk’s plan for datacenters in space
US federal regulators approved a constellation of datacenters to process data in space today, saying that they would “support America’s booming super intelligence economy”.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said in a statement that regulators had approved 1m Starmind orbital satellites, or compute modules, built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. It is the first such authorization in US history.
The FCC said that the authorization “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.
“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” said the FCC chair, Brendan Carr.
Boosters of the plan have argued that datacenters in space are essential as the AI industry grows and their cost on Earth on the power grid and water supply are high.

“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial datacenters,” SpaceX had argued to the FCC.
But critics say the technology for such space datacenters is still being developed, and their deployment is a long way off.

Under the license approved today, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number – or 100,000 – no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.
Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under investigation before reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
JD Vance has said that he was assured by the US Department of Justice that Jensen Huang “was under no investigation” ahead of his surprise reinstatement as Nvidia CEO yesterday.
Speaking to reporters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, the vice-president said:
double quotation markWe received assurances that he was under no investigation.
“It was ultimately the board’s decision to bring Jensen Huang back,” he added, a day after Donald Trump took credit for “convincing” Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstall Huang as chief executive.

Trump earlier today expressed he’d be open to pardoning Huang for potential crimes but didn’t think it would be necessary. Asked about that, Vance replied, “Well, I don’t think he needs a pardon at all,” as, he said, there was no evidence that Huang committed a crime.
Nvidia’s products are a very important part of the “SI race”, , Vance continued (referring to Trump’s preferred term “super-intelligence”, rather than “artificial intelligence”).

“We really do care about those chips not falling into the wrong hands,” Vance said, adding this was an opportunity for Nvidia “to focus on complying with American export controls and we think Jensen Huang is going to take it very seriously.”

Earlier, Reuters reported that the US justice department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations Huang conducted an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Instead, attorney general Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the DOJ’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said Reuters’ sources.

That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was reportedly crucial to Blanche’s decision to tell Trump and Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security.

Speaking to reporters today, Sandoval-Moshenberg confirmed that US district judge Paula Xinis ordered the federal government to “withdraw all impediments” for Abrego Garcia to leave the country — including a GPS ankle monitor. In exchange Abrego Garcia was required to leave the US by 24 November.

“I’ll just share candidly that when we tried to check him in online on Monday, we couldn’t do it,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said. “And then on Tuesday, we were able to because the government had, presumably, complied with the judge’s order to take him off of any sort of no fly list.”
'I feel free of everything evil': Kilmar Abrego speaks to reporters just hours after arriving in Spain
Kilmar Abrego Garcia told reporters on Wednesday that he feels “free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point”.
“I’m happy this time because this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely,” Abrego Garcia said on a press call just hours after arriving in Madrid, Spain.
He added: “The government did did not decide where my story continues. My family and I decide our future.”

Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been living in Maryland, was deported by the Trump administration to Cecot last, the country’s notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, even though a court had barred his removal to El Salvador because of gang threats against his family.

“I’m glad that the Trump administration did not succeed at what they wanted to do,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to El Salvador to visit Abrego Garcia in April last year. “They wanted to leave him there to rot for the rest of his life. Instead, we saw our judicial system work alongside a strong legal team to produce this outcome, where Kilmar Abrego Garcia is able to chart his own future.”

Van Hollen, who is vying to become Senate majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress next year, has made Abrego Garcia’s case and opposition to the administration’s sweeping deportation crackdown central to his vision for the party.

“Abrego Garcia’s journey is an example of our Constitution working despite the attacks of the Trump administration,” Van Hollen added. He said he had spoken with the Spanish ambassador to the United States, Ángeles Moreno Bau, and briefed her on “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration against Kilmar Abrego Garcia”, adding that he was pleased Abrego Garcia was now in Spain and able to continue telling his story”.

Abrego Garcia, who is married to a US citizen and shares a young son with her, was returned to the United States following a supreme court ruling. The administration has since sought to deport him again, exploring transfers to several African countries.

“Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, Abrego Garcia’s co-counsel. “Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus. And there’s really no other way to see this other than Mr Abrego Garcia’s decision to hold strong throughout the last two years of this process.”

Sandoval-Moshenberg said his legal team would eventually be able to disclose Abrego Garcia’s next destination after Spain, but added that a pathway exists for him to obtain permanent residency in the United States in the near future.
“This is a short-term absence from the US,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.
While Abrego Garcia did not take questions on Wednesday, he underscored the need to “keep fighting”.
“I’m happy. My family’s with me. There’s a tremendous community with me,” he said.
The Trump administration did not open a formal investigation into Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO, before Donald Trump urged the board to reinstate him, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Instead, Todd Blanche, the attorney general, concluded the Justice Department (DOJ) had no evidence to indicate Huang broke any laws based on the department’s ongoing investigations into two of Nvidia’s clients, including Megaspeed International – the company suspected of smuggling chips into China.

Blanche was vague with reporters on Tuesday, refusing to directly say whether the DOJ had conducted an investigation, instead claiming law enforcement “looked into” the situation to make a final determination.
The probe of Nvidia’s clients found no evidence that Huang acted as an agent of China or provided sensitive information about semiconductors to China, sources told Reuters.

Donald Trump insisted, on Wednesday, that stocks were down “because of the November Third Election results” rather than waning confidence in AI and tech companies, new tariff proposals or rising inflation.

“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results. I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING. I told you so!!!” Trump wrote, indirectly blaming the Democratic Party’s sweeping wins earlier this month.
However, other facts appear to be contributing to the stock market’s performance.
Inflation rose 3.7% in October, – the highest rate since May, according to a report released on Wednesday.

Additionally, the Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including the European Union and China, on Wednesday. The US trade representative also proposed adding a 20% tax to Chinese imports, bringing the total tax to 40%.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index also fluctuated in the wake of drama over Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. Despite being reinstalled as the company’s leader, the Nasdaq was down by more than two percentage points.
